column1: Product Learnings Observed During Manual Retrieval
These are product-design observations, not blind-test evidence. They capture how expert retrieval actually works.

column2: Query text alone is sometimes insufficient to judge relevance; the researcher may need to open the search and inspect the intent revealed by the results.
column3: The retrieval layer may need a controlled 'probe this branch' action before deciding expand vs stop, rather than relying only on lexical similarity.
column4: 'MRI safety list' initially looked relevant, but opening it revealed implant/manufacturer-list intent and the branch was then stopped.

column2: Business/SME context materially changes retrieval relevance.
column3: The product needs business-scope context before deciding whether a query is relevant; generic SEO relevance is not enough.
column4: MRI safety certification was rejected because the business does not certify; MRI safety course remained relevant because the business trains healthcare workers.

column2: A useful stopping rule is saturation: close a branch when it converges into repeats, variants or peripheral intents rather than continuing indefinitely.
column3: The retrieval engine needs a saturation/novelty stop condition, not just a fixed keyword count or depth limit.
column4: The 'MRI safety guidelines for staff' branch was closed once related searches mostly repeated PPT, certification, ACR manuals, implants and already-covered safety queries.

column2: Repeated appearances across branches should be preserved conceptually as recurrence, even when the working tree de-duplicates the literal query rows.
column3: Recurrence may later be a qualitative signal, but should not be falsely converted into search volume.
column4: MRI safety PPT, radiology, articles and guideline terms reappeared across multiple branches.

column2: A relevant parent query can still terminate quickly when its child results are only format modifiers or repetitions.
column3: The retrieval engine should not assume every relevant query deserves deep expansion; novelty matters at every level.
column4: MRI safety PPT was relevant, but its child results mostly repeated PDF, SlideShare, precautions and staff-guideline variants, so the branch closed.

column2: Training intent needs business-offer and geography filters, not just topical relevance.
column3: The product brain must use business scope + target market to separate course demand from certification systems or country-specific training frameworks.
column4: MRI safety course / free / online / India / near me were kept; Level 1/2, NHS and certificate queries were rejected.

column2: A seed can be declared complete when every open branch has either saturated, been ruled out by business scope, or produced no new underlying intent.
column3: The retrieval stage needs an explicit seed-level completion condition so the agent can stop confidently.
column4: The main 'MRI safety' seed was closed after PDF, PPT, list, radiology and course branches all converged or terminated.

column2: A synonym/near-synonym seed can be used as a coverage check, but should be stopped quickly if it produces the same query universe.
column3: The retrieval engine should test alternate seed phrasings for novelty, then terminate them when they add no new meaningful branch.
column4: 'mri safe' largely repeated 'mri safety' results; only a couple of new surface forms appeared, so the seed was closed.

column2: Existing product catalogues are useful for generating seed queries, but they are not themselves evidence that those products deserve dedicated website pages.
column3: The retrieval system should use the catalogue to propose candidate seeds, then independently test each seed against real search evidence before architecture decisions are made.
column4: The current site menu contains products such as MRI Monitoring System, MRI Infusion Pump, MRI Safe Fire Extinguisher, MRI Furniture and MRI Accessories.

column2: A broad product-category seed can reveal a usable product taxonomy even when its related-search results are noisy or implant-heavy.
column3: The retrieval engine should use autocomplete as a product-discovery source alongside Related Searches/PAA, because autocomplete may surface commercially meaningful product names directly.
column4: 'mri compatible' surfaced pulse oximeter, monitor, laryngoscope, ventilator, ECG electrodes, wheelchair, anesthesia machine and fire extinguisher.

column2: Commercial modifiers such as 'price' and 'price in India' can confirm product-shopping intent without requiring search-volume data.
column3: The reasoning layer should preserve commercial/geographic modifiers as intent evidence while avoiding generic non-MRI price queries.
column4: 'MRI Compatible Pulse Oximeter Price in India' was relevant, while generic 'How much does a pulse oximeter cost in India?' was rejected.

column2: The same topical keyword can split into useful institutional-product intent versus irrelevant patient/implant/manufacturer intent.
column3: Business context must be applied after retrieval so the model can keep MRI-compatible hospital equipment while rejecting pacemakers, implants, brand checkers and patient questions.
column4: Pulse oximeter, ventilator, wheelchair and anesthesia machine were kept; pacemaker, implants, Medtronic/EMCO and patient jewellery/bra questions were rejected.

column2: One equipment family can have several commercially equivalent search names plus subtypes.
column3: The clustering layer must merge true synonyms/near-synonyms while preserving subtype distinctions that may affect page architecture.
column4: MRI-compatible monitor, MRI patient monitor, MRI-safe monitor and monitoring equipment are near-synonyms; multipara/multiparameter and cardiac monitor are meaningful subtype terms.

column2: Brand/model searches are useful market vocabulary even when the business is not the dealer for every brand.
column3: The raw evidence should retain brand/model demand, but manuals/service-document intent should usually stop unless the business explicitly supports that job.
column4: IRadimed, Mindray, Tesla M3, Invivo Expression and Philips were retained as market vocabulary; IRadimed/Tesla service manuals were rejected.

column2: A product branch can surface adjacent product seeds that should be queued rather than forced into the current cluster.
column3: The retrieval engine should hand off strong cross-product discoveries into a seed backlog so one branch does not become an unbounded mixed taxonomy.
column4: The monitor branch surfaced MRI anesthesia machine, MRI-compatible infusion pump price, ventilator price/circuit and MRI-compatible display.

column2: Commercial modifiers remain relevant only when the MRI/product qualifier is preserved.
column3: The system should distinguish 'MRI Compatible Patient Monitor Price' from generic patient-monitor or medical-display price questions.
column4: MRI-compatible monitor price was retained; generic patient-monitor cost, 27-inch monitor cost and 3-para price PAA were rejected.

column2: Product searches can reveal accessory demand around a core device, but accessory relevance may depend on what the business actually stocks.
column3: The product brain should keep accessory variants provisionally, then use catalogue/SME context before deciding whether they deserve coverage.
column4: MRI-compatible laryngoscope surfaced set, battery, blades and handle variants.

column2: Competitor/brand context may need to be an explicit business input rather than inferred only from search results.
column3: A competitor-brand field could help the reasoning layer distinguish useful comparative/brand demand from irrelevant brands without suppressing genuine market vocabulary.
column4: Penlon surfaced repeatedly as an MRI-compatible laryngoscope brand; the user noted this as a grey area and suggested capturing competitor brands.

column2: A product branch can surface genuinely new adjacent equipment categories that should be queued rather than explored immediately.
column3: The seed backlog is important for breadth-first coverage while preventing one branch from becoming unbounded.
column4: MRI-compatible laryngoscope surfaced MRI-compatible suction machine and MRI-compatible vaporizer as separate product seeds.

column2: MRI qualification is a strong relevance boundary: once a query drifts into generic product categories or procedures, it should usually stop.
column3: The retrieval layer should preserve MRI-qualified commercial/product variants while cutting generic price, EMS, pediatric, flexible-video and procedure-cost branches.
column4: MRI Compatible Laryngoscope Price and Penlon MRI Laryngoscope were retained; generic Laryngoscope price, Video Laryngoscope Price and flexible-laryngoscopy cost were rejected.

column2: Small product branches can be valuable even when they close quickly, because they may reveal adjacent equipment categories.
column3: The retrieval engine should treat branch closure and seed discovery as separate outcomes: a branch can be 'done' while still contributing new seeds to the backlog.
column4: MRI-compatible suction machine closed quickly but surfaced flow meter, oxygen flowmeter, anesthesia machine and MRI ventilator terms.

column2: Running an MRI-safe/MRI-compatible synonym check is useful for coverage, but repeated terms should not trigger duplicate exploration.
column3: The retrieval layer should use synonym checks to detect missing vocabulary and then de-duplicate against already explored nodes.
column4: 'MRI safe suction machine' mostly returned already-covered laryngoscope/anesthesia/flowmeter themes.

column2: Brand-price queries can remain useful commercial vocabulary even when manuals/support queries from the same brand should be excluded.
column3: The reasoning layer needs intent-level filtering within the same brand rather than blanket inclusion or exclusion of brand searches.
column4: Penlon Vaporizer Price was retained; Penlon Sigma Delta vaporizer User manual was rejected.

column2: A valid product seed may have little or no search fan-out and still remain relevant as a leaf.
column3: The retrieval engine should distinguish 'no further expansion' from 'irrelevant'; a small branch can close cleanly without being discarded.
column4: MRI-compatible flow meter and MRI-compatible oxygen flowmeter produced no useful PAA/related-search expansion but remained valid product terms.

column2: Brand/model strings can be ambiguous without explicit catalogue or competitor context.
column3: The product should preserve observed brand/model vocabulary in raw evidence while allowing business context to decide whether it matters for the final architecture.
column4: Penlon Prima 451 MRI and Penlon anesthesia machine appeared under the anesthesia-machine branch, but the user chose not to pursue them.

column2: Adding the target geography to a major product seed is a useful coverage check, but it can cause Google to drift into generic local demand.
column3: Run a geography-modified check for major product branches, then retain only results that preserve both the product and MRI-specific intent.
column4: 'mri compatible ventilator india' mostly produced generic portable/transport ventilator terms, so they were rejected.

column2: Synonym and geography checks are best treated as coverage tests rather than automatic new branches.
column3: This catches missing vocabulary without creating duplicate exploration before a seed is declared complete.
column4: MRI-safe ventilator and MRI-compatible ventilator India were checked before closing the ventilator seed.

column2: Alphabetic autocomplete probing (for example typing 'mri compatible e') can surface product/accessory families that broad category searches do not expose cleanly.
column3: The retrieval layer may benefit from controlled prefix expansion after a major umbrella term, while still requiring business-context filtering before treating every suggestion as relevant.
column4: The 'e' probe surfaced ECG leads/electrodes, EEG leads/electrodes, extinguisher and external fixator.

column2: Very small product branches can still validate a product term and surface one useful adjacent seed.
column3: The system should close a branch once the core synonym/commercial modifiers are exhausted, while handing off any genuinely new product category.
column4: MRI-compatible wheelchair yielded safe/safety synonyms, price/cost and one new adjacent seed: MRI-compatible stretcher.

column2: B2B relevance can depend on buyer type, not just topic match.
column3: Business context should distinguish institutional procurement intent from end-user retail/specification intent even when both mention the same MRI-safe product.
column4: Wheelchair price/cost were retained, while 'for sale', parts and weight-limit queries were rejected because the business does not sell to end users.

column2: Product + geography is a recurring modifier across branches, but local variants can appear at several levels (India, Delhi, Noida).
column3: The retrieval layer should test a standard geography modifier for each major product seed and preserve local commercial intent without mistaking it for search volume.
column4: Fire-extinguisher research surfaced price in India, near Delhi and near Noida; wheelchair research reinforced the same 'product + India' pattern.

column2: A strong synonym can expose a second useful keyword universe even when the product is the same.
column3: The clustering layer should merge true synonyms while preserving distinctive modifiers discovered under each synonym.
column4: MRI-compatible, MRI-safe and non-magnetic all described the fire-extinguisher product family, with non-magnetic surfacing types/manufacturers/best queries.

column2: Informational modifiers around a B2B product can still be useful as supporting/FAQ demand even when they are not separate commercial pages.
column3: The gold-standard stage should distinguish page-worthy commercial intent from supporting informational intent instead of discarding the latter.
column4: Fire-extinguisher color, class, sign and 'Which fire extinguisher is compatible with MRI scanners?' were retained as useful informational evidence.

column2: The same brand/manufacturer concept may be relevant in one context and irrelevant in another, so later explicit judgement should override earlier tentative calls.
column3: The decision log must preserve updates rather than treating early relevance calls as immutable.
column4: Safex manufacturer was initially considered useful, then later rejected when the user refined the branch.

column2: A product family can have both functional subtypes and strong brand/model vocabulary without requiring separate architecture for every brand.
column3: The gold-standard step should separate product-family structure (infusion pump, syringe pump, IV pump) from brand/model evidence (B. Braun, IRadimed, MRidium).
column4: MRI-compatible infusion pump surfaced syringe/IV variants plus B. Braun, IRadimed and MRidium terms.

column2: Cross-product terms frequently reappear inside another product branch and should be routed back to their existing cluster instead of treated as new demand.
column3: The reasoning layer needs cross-cluster de-duplication across the entire research set, not just within one seed.
column4: The infusion-pump branch resurfaced MRI patient monitor, IRadimed monitor price, Mindray anesthesia machine and MRI-compatible fire extinguisher.

column2: Subtype education can be relevant even when it does not create a new commercial page.
column3: The gold standard should preserve informational questions that clarify product selection while keeping them distinct from dedicated product-page demand.
column4: 'What is the difference between an infusion pump and a syringe pump?' was retained as supporting informational evidence.

column2: Some catalogue categories are valid search concepts but have almost no query fan-out beyond one obvious subtype.
column3: The retrieval engine should allow a category to close as a small leaf without forcing artificial depth or inventing additional products.
column4: MRI-compatible furniture produced essentially one useful subtype, MRI-compatible chair, then saturated.

column2: The raw-retrieval phase should end at saturation, not after every catalogue item or every possible Google branch has been exhausted.
column3: For the experiment, the dataset is sufficient once major business categories have been covered and new searches mostly produce repeats, generic drift or tiny leaf branches.
column4: Accessories, furniture, wheelchair/stretcher, fire extinguisher, infusion pump, ventilator and Faraday-cage checks increasingly produced either repeats or one-node leaves.

column2: Business-created services may be strategically important even when Google offers little fan-out.
column3: The system needs business context alongside demand evidence so a commercially important service is not discarded just because the query universe is small.
column4: MRI Faraday cage / MRI room Faraday cage is a real business service despite limited search expansion.

column2: Uncertain new categories should remain explicitly unassessed instead of being forced into the gold standard.
column3: This prevents the expert answer key from being contaminated by guesses and gives the product a clean 'needs business confirmation' state.
column4: MRI entertainment system, MRI-safe TV, MRI shielding and RF interference MRI remain unassessed.

column2: Manual Google-only demand retrieval for this niche category took about five hours even for an experienced marketer who knew the business.
column3: Time cost is part of the product opportunity: the value is not only better synthesis, but compressing a multi-hour expert research workflow into a much shorter guided run.
column4: User worked roughly 2:00–6:00 and 8:30–9:30 on the MRI-safety raw-research pass.

column2: Price/cost and similar evaluation modifiers are middle-of-funnel consideration signals, even when they sit under a bottom-of-funnel product family.
column3: If evaluated as their own query intent, classify price, cost, availability, lead-time, best and manufacturer queries as MOFU; normally satisfy them on the same BOFU product-family page rather than creating separate thin pages.
column4: Ventilator price, wheelchair cost, fire-extinguisher price and infusion-pump price should inform their product pages without becoming standalone price pages.

column2: Keyword depth should not be used as a proxy for whether a product is a major equipment family.
column3: Use business/product ontology to distinguish complete machines from accessories; search evidence informs demand and language, not the physical/product hierarchy by itself.
column4: MRI-compatible anesthesia machines and suction machines are major equipment families even though their Google branches were smaller.

column2: Commercial vs transactional intent and funnel stage are separate dimensions.
column3: A category query can be Commercial because the user is browsing options, yet still be BOFU because they are already seeking a specific class of purchasable MRI products. MOFU is reserved for consideration/evaluation signals such as price, availability, lead time, best and manufacturers.
column4: MRI-compatible accessories = Commercial / BOFU; MRI-compatible stethoscope = Transactional / BOFU; accessory pricing = Commercial / MOFU.

column2: Some offerings combine a physical system with implementation/installation and should not be forced into a pure product-vs-service binary.
column3: Allow a 'Product-service page' treatment in the website architecture.
column4: MRI Faraday Cage & RF Shielding is a physical shielding system plus manufacture/installation.

column2: Cross-cutting modifiers such as price, best, manufacturer, availability and geography should usually enrich product pages rather than create separate thin pages.
column3: Treat these as MOFU consideration sub-intents nested inside BOFU category/product-family/product pages; brand/model searches can justify product-detail pages only when the business actually carries those models.
column4: The MRI dataset repeatedly surfaced price/cost, India/local, manufacturer/best and brand/model terms across multiple product families.

column2: The blind test should score the risky demand-to-architecture reasoning, not generic website hygiene.
column3: Keep baseline utility pages such as Home, About and Contact outside the Core-miss rule; score demand-derived pages/needs and reasonable architecture decisions.
column4: This prevents a generic site checklist from distorting the experiment while still allowing the AI to propose standard utility pages.

column2: A broad supplier/dealer query can provide the missing demand-led job for the home page.
column3: When a query spans the whole catalogue and company rather than one product family, use it to frame the home page rather than forcing it into a category page.
column4: MRI-compatible equipment dealer in India / MRI-safe equipment dealers, product dealers and sellers in India became the demand-derived homepage target.

column2: Not every product-related FAQ is useful for a specialist catalogue.
column3: If the business exclusively sells MRI-safe/MRI-compatible equipment, generic 'is this equipment MRI compatible?' questions do not need to shape acquisition architecture; keep only FAQs that help selection, specification or purchase.
column4: Compatibility-check questions were removed from the gold standard, while fire-extinguisher class/type/sign questions remain useful evaluation content.

column2: The official blind run failed the precommitted keep-rate threshold even though all Core underlying needs were covered.
column3: Treat Core-need coverage and page-architecture quality as separate checks; good demand understanding does not guarantee usable IA.
column4: Gemini: 8 of 13 proposed page/content areas kept (61.5%); no Core gold-standard need completely missed.

column2: More reasoning compute did not remove the architecture-granularity problem.
column3: The product needs an explicit correction checkpoint for product/content hierarchy rather than assuming a stronger model will reliably choose the right page granularity.
column4: Gemini over-merged distinct product families; Claude Opus 5.5 High preserved product distinctions better but overbuilt informational pages.

column2: The AI can be strong at cleaning, relevance filtering and identifying underlying demand while still being unreliable at the final merge/split decision.
column3: Separate the workflow into provisional demand/product grouping -> practitioner Correct/Fix this -> final website architecture.
column4: This is now the clearest product-design implication from both blind runs.

column2: Query recurrence or breadth is not search volume.
column3: High / Medium / Low demand must come from external volume data such as DataForSEO; where reliable volume is unavailable, show 'Insufficient evidence'.
column4: Both blind models used qualitative evidence patterns to infer priority, reinforcing the need for a hard guardrail.

column2: The MRI manual-research benchmark is approximately five hours before synthesis and architecture review.
column3: The product opportunity includes compressing retrieval and synthesis time while preserving the marketer's authority over consequential grouping decisions.
column4: Manual raw research was approximately 2:00–6:00 plus 8:30–9:30.
